title: AI 2040 isn't about stopping AI, it's about pushing superintelligence to 2040
dek: The real mechanism behind the anti-AI proposal is a compute cap: pause new frontier training, allow inference only, and make stealing weights impossible with a 1 MB/s external link and a Faraday cage.
why: High information density, but the topics jump around: AI regulation, robotics, how VCs read people, and the chip supply chain each get a segment, so it's good for picking and choosing.
who: Founders and investors watching AI regulation, robotics and the chip supply chain; practitioners who want to understand how VCs read people and where personal agents are heading.
skip: If you're not interested in music-industry people-reading stories, you can skip the Guy Oseary segment from 22:10 to 28:45.

points.h: AI 2040 doesn't stop AI, it delays it to 2040
points.body: Many people assume anti-AI sentiment is pushing to ‘stop AI’, but what the AI 2040 proposal actually says is: keep inference on existing models, keep doing capability research, just push superintelligence from 2028 to 2040. The concrete mechanism is a compute cap — pause new frontier training, apply ‘inference-only verification’ to data centers above 10,000 H100-equivalents (roughly $100M of equipment), and physically rip out the high-bandwidth east-west networking inside the data center so distributed training can't run but inference proceeds as normal. New R&D centers would have to be built from scratch inside a Faraday cage, with external connectivity capped at 1 MB/s — stealing the weights would take five years.

points.h: Anti-AI mobilization is nowhere near anti-battery-chicken
points.body: Speaker 2 points out a contrast: the anti-flock (anti-battery-chicken) movement converts into real physical action by ordinary people, whereas on the anti-AI side you don't see a 100,000-like video teaching people ‘how to cut power to your local data center’. Speaker 1 adds that the volume on the anti-AI side comes more from concrete interests like ‘I'm an artist and I don't like AI-generated images’ than from x-risk arguments. Data centers are in remote locations, fenced and heavily fortified — far harder to get at than a chicken coop on the street.

points.h: The compute cap is the valve easiest to turn
points.body: The most effective control lever in the proposal is judged to be the compute cap: chip controls plus slower data center construction. The goal is to make models stronger mainly by adding hardware rather than by new algorithms — because algorithmic breakthroughs can be hidden inside secret projects. Speaker 1 notes that Ilya's new lab recently got a large cluster from NVIDIA; even people on an orthogonal research path have to stack compute, which shows that ‘scale is a prerequisite’ is basically consensus in this circle.

points.h: Doomers don't bet, because they wouldn't live to collect
points.body: Tyler Cowen demands that pessimists name the corresponding market price to validate their beliefs, but Deep Dish pushes back: why should short-term existential risk be reflected in market prices? ‘If everyone's dead, the contract that pays out is worthless to me.’ Speaker 5 twists the knife: in the nuclear-war era people built bunkers; nobody builds an AI bunker, because everyone thinks it's too totalizing for a bunker to help — so ‘you didn't build a bunker’ doesn't prove you don't believe. Paul Christiano is dug up as being 2x levered long and short 30-year US Treasuries, but that bet also makes money in the ‘good ending’, unlike a doomsday wager.

points.h: The fruit-fly agent moves the moral question forward
points.body: Google mapped out all the neurons of a fruit fly, and once the code was open-sourced people started messing with it in every way: someone put the fruit-fly agent inside a Rabbit R1, and shaking the device makes its escape circuit light up; someone else had it play Doom. Speaker 1 thinks the real question is the next stop on this road — if you can simulate a person, hold a conversation, behave like a person, does it have moral status? His own judgment is not to overthink it and not to be in the business of torturing anything. He also mentions having Astra play Balatro with computer use last night, and it felt like giving it a reward rather than torturing it.

points.h: Once a reporter is in the room, he stops being escorted out
points.body: Alex Heath describes the core mechanism of his changed status: when a reporter is in the room, you're brought in and then immediately escorted out; now he gets to stay in the room and slowly marinate on it. So his newsletter perspective changes — it's not about landing a scoop, but about letting a large volume of off-the-record conversation settle into a judgment, like the personal agents piece he's writing. He says explicitly that confidentiality still matters and he won't leak memos companies are worried about again; ten years in, that's enough.

points.h: A newcomer can hardly replicate his path now
points.body: Asked whether now is a good time to become the next Alex Heath, his answer is the opposite: the traditional media environment is structurally challenged, many places aren't hiring, traffic is falling, and they haven't shifted to direct models like subscriptions and streaming. The only viable path he offers is ‘maniacally focus on one thing and become the best in the world at that’ — he himself started by focusing on covering Snap, broke a pile of Snap news, and after being noticed migrated that capability to other companies. And the niche has to be the intersection of niche and matters, not just obscure.

points.h: Fear of being left behind hands new players an opening
points.body: One of the hosts besides Mitesh proposes a counterintuitive mechanism: because people fear AI, they're more willing to try new products — they don't want to be left behind, don't want to become a permanent underclass. The result is that people who've used various AI products for years are still willing to try new things, which keeps creating an advantage for second and third entrants. At the same time, once an AI brand gets big it starts accumulating baggage, and people become more willing to share and discuss something new rather than the one they use every day. That leaves a lot of room for startups.

points.h: The endgame for personal agents is network effects
points.body: The discussion compares personal agents with the inference market for frontier models: every company will build a personal agent, and many already have. The key disagreement is whether this is a network-effects business — one side thinks yes, and that it can eventually take a cut of agentic commerce, e.g. you buy a car through it and it earns $500; Zuck has also said take rate is his business. The other side offers a counterexample: an agent isn't a person, so you may not care whether it's in the network; but if a given agent has never leaked, never crashed, never been hacked, you will indeed stay.

points.h: The window to rebuild social networks is opening
points.body: One concrete judgment: now may be the best time to rebuild a social network, because you can have your agent open your Snap or LinkedIn, pull out every single person in there — they have no say in it — and add them back on the new network. The old arbitrage window of ‘export your contacts’ closed; now it's reopening. The immediate criticism: the old critique of social media was ‘we built social media for socializing, and it made people less social’; in the personal-agent era the new critique becomes ‘nobody talks to people anymore, only agents talk to each other’, and even chatting with grandma about a road trip becomes ‘talk to my agent’.

points.h: Chip companies are now asked whether they can build it
points.body: Mitesh says that walking into a meeting room at a hyperscaler or frontier lab, the question isn't performance but two things: first, can you build enough of it — is the supply chain and component base robust enough; second, can you deploy it — does it need liquid cooling, and if so they may not have a data center for it, because it's already allocated to GPUs or TPUs. The threshold number he gives is gigawatt plus; at that scale, even counting ASICs as cheaper, it's tens of billions of dollars. His own cadence is tape out this year, volume ramp in the second half of 2027, and a plan to reach several hundred megawatts in 2028.

points.h: Using commodity memory to bypass the HBM and CoWoS bottleneck
points.body: Positron's technical route is to bypass the queue for HBM and CoWoS — NVIDIA, TPU and AMD are all ahead of you. The approach is to use commodity memory, at the cost of being slow, so the technical innovation lies in how to solve the slowness. But commodity memory isn't freely available either; you can't just walk up to Samsung or Micron and ask for LPDDR5x, you still have to plan. He mentions the first-generation product was built on FPGA, with fewer than 20 people, delivering to the first customer in 15 months; Oracle now has 50 Atlas racks; the company just passed 100 people, more than 50 of whom joined in the last three months.

points.h: The robot takes one to two hours to draw a picture
points.body: Thijs hooked Codex directly up to a Hugging Face open-source robotic arm to draw the TBPN logo; one drawing takes one to two hours, and he says himself it's ‘probably quite expensive’ and ‘definitely pretty slow’. His approach isn't to have the model look at an image and make one move, but to first have the model write a plan in the form of code, execute it, then take a picture every few seconds to monitor in the background and fine-tune the plan. He judges that a high-frequency image–small action–image loop would perform best, but the current ‘plan first, then monitor’ is a speed compromise.

points.h: Robotic arms went from thousands of dollars to two hundred
points.body: Thijs says traditional robot hardware costs thousands to tens of thousands of dollars, whereas the Hugging Face SO-100 behind him is open-source, fully 3D-printable, and only requires buying actuators separately — currently about $200 (he adds that this price is on the high side, caused by supply chain issues). He compares it to the 3D printing boom: before industrial-grade machines became widespread, people would first buy these cheap plastic arms to clamp on a desk, plug in an off-the-shelf agent and use it.

points.h: Guy Oseary put nearly a billion dollars into OpenAI and Anthropic
points.body: Guy Oseary says that when he invested in Anthropic and OpenAI, they may have been the only fund betting that deep, and many people were confused at the time, but they were convinced these were long-term foundational platforms. He reveals they added more in the two companies' later rounds, for a cumulative total approaching $1 billion. But he also says that telling what's real from what isn't is far harder today than it was then — ‘It's not as easy as it was for us to really decipher’.

points.h: Listen to a pitch the way you listen to a song: find the chorus
points.body: Guy Oseary equates spotting founders with collecting demo tapes in clubs back in the day: at 17 he had 100 demos in hand, and the ones initially ranked top three had fallen out of the top 20 by the time he reached the 100th. He says he listens to every pitch like a song or an album, and the test is ‘is there a chorus’ — ‘I'm always listening for the chorus’; if he can't hear a chorus, he thinks the song doesn't work. Alanis Morissette played 30 to 40 seconds of Perfect in his office and he decided to sign her; Muse flew in from London, and after the first song he stopped them and said they could start.

points.h: Alex Heath spots fakes by having met the very best
points.body: Alex Heath says he can see through marketing at a glance because he's spent a long time around the world's top founders — he just did Zuckerberg, and before that Sam Altman. Once you've seen people at the apex, with high integrity, dominating on the field, you can quickly tell who's pretending. He says he often has the instinct that ‘this looks like it'll pop’, and it's been right often enough. Guy adds that this instinct came from having to move fast back then: if you didn't decide to sign an artist immediately, Jimmy Iovine would outbid you and take them.

terms.def: A regulatory plan that would pause new frontier training, allow inference only, and push superintelligence to 2040.
Hugging Face's open-source, 3D-printable desktop robotic arm, about $200.
General-purpose memory such as LPDDR5x, used instead of HBM to bypass the CoWoS queue.
TSMC's advanced packaging technology, required to integrate HBM with GPUs, with tight capacity.
A data center power threshold; at this scale even ASICs require tens of billions of dollars.
